2ec5dbc0-a359-49aa-8def-1c82ef17b9bf.implications: For a repo/rates desk, Hunt's thesis points toward a structurally higher and more volatile long-end rate regime and widening Treasury term/risk premium as deficit and interest-expense dynamics worsen — relevant to duration positioning, collateral supply dynamics, and front-end Fed-policy expectations, though his M2/velocity framework is idiosyncratic and not the market consensus.
key_claims: Hunt: FY just ended budget deficit was 6.3% of GDP versus a ~1.5% historical average for late-cycle expansions since 1960
Hunt: October 2025 interest expense was just under 20% of total federal revenues, and could reach ~20% of the total budget within about five years
Hunt: M2 money supply has grown at a 6.5% annualized rate since December, versus his calculated non-inflationary benchmark of roughly 3-3.25%
Hunt: core PCE inflation has run above the Fed's 2% target for 67-68 consecutive months, with services inflation above 4%
Hunt: a typical recession would push the deficit from 6% to over 10% of GDP, given deficits have historically widened ~4 percentage points in downturns

2ec5dbc0-a359-49aa-8def-1c82ef17b9bf.one_liner: A veteran economist argues the Fed is accelerating money growth into an already-entrenched inflation problem while the fiscal deficit becomes structurally unmanageable, implying a sustained rise in long-end yields and Treasury risk premia.
2ec5dbc0-a359-49aa-8def-1c82ef17b9bf.recap: Dr. Lacey Hunt of Hoisington Investment Management tells Julia La Roche this is the most worried he's been in his 57-year career, despite the economy being at a late-cycle boom with low unemployment and record consumer/capital spending. His central concern is the federal budget deficit, which hit 6.3% of GDP in the last fiscal year versus a historical late-expansion norm of about 1.5% — four times worse than comparable prior periods. He calculates interest expense was already near 20% of federal revenues in October and projects it could hit 20% of the total budget within roughly five years, driven by rising debt and rising rates. He argues the deficit is politically intractable (citing Nobel laureate James Buchanan's work on democracies' inability to run surpluses in good times), and that any recession would push the deficit toward 10-10.5% of GDP, overwhelming national saving. On inflation, Hunt says M2 has grown at a 6.5% annualized rate since December versus his calculated non-inflationary benchmark of roughly 3-3.25% (potential growth plus Fed's 2% target, adjusted for rising velocity). He draws parallels to the Burns-era Fed of the 1970s, arguing inflation is not mean-reverting once embedded, and that the US has had 67-68 months of above-target inflation. He attributes the end of the disinflationary era to deglobalization/reshoring reversing prior economies-of-scale benefits, and warns of gradual erosion of dollar reserve-currency status and rising Treasury risk premia as foreign central banks diversify into gold.
terms: M2 -- a broad measure of US money supply including cash, checking/savings deposits, and retail money market funds
CPI -- Consumer Price Index, a measure of inflation based on a basket of consumer goods and services
PCE -- Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge
CBO -- Congressional Budget Office, the nonpartisan US agency that scores federal budget and legislative costs

a753bb1e-e2b4-11f1-a386-47d9a7ead080.implications: For a rates/repo trader, the key signal is that Goldman expects fewer Fed/ECB/BoE hikes than the market is pricing, sees bond returns as attractively asymmetric into 2027 (high running yield plus room for yields to fall), and flags French fiscal/political risk and AI-capex deceleration as the catalysts most likely to move front-end and long-end rates; credit is expected to modestly underperform but without a dramatic deterioration.
key_claims: Goldman estimates 2026 global growth at 2.7%, in line with potential, and forecasts 2.8% for 2027 (Jan Hatzius)
AI investment added about 0.5% to global GDP in 2026, concentrated in Taiwan, Korea and the US (Hatzius)
Tariff pass-through is still adding about 40bp to year-on-year core PCE inflation; Goldman expects core PCE at 2.4% by end-2027 (Hatzius)
Fed expected to hike 25bp in December 2026 and once more in Q1 2027 (likely March), capping tightening below current market pricing (Hatzius)
ECB expected to hike once in December with risk of one more in 2027; BoE one hike in early 2027; BoJ seen delivering three hikes to a 2% terminal rate, at or above market pricing (Hatzius)
Oil risk premium has compressed from about $30 a few weeks ago to near zero, leaving the market more exposed to renewed escalation risk (Dominic Wilson)
Goldman sees bond return prospects as the most attractive since 2020, given higher running yields plus expected gradual yield declines through 2027 (Wilson)
2027 baseline: positive but more modest equity and bond returns, modest credit underperformance, flattish-to-slightly-negative commodity returns (Wilson)
a753bb1e-e2b4-11f1-a386-47d9a7ead080.one_liner: Goldman's 2027 outlook centers on Fed hikes (not cuts), sticky inflation from tariffs/energy, and a friendlier bond-return backdrop once the hiking cycle caps out -- core reading for a rates desk even though repo/funding plumbing isn't directly addressed.
a753bb1e-e2b4-11f1-a386-47d9a7ead080.recap: Goldman's chief economist Jan Hatzius and senior advisor Dominic Wilson review 2026 and preview 2027. Global growth held at ~2.7% in 2026 despite tariffs, the Iran war, and higher rates, cushioned by expansionary fiscal policy (US, Germany, Asian fuel subsidies) and an AI investment boom adding roughly half a percentage point to global GDP. For 2027 Goldman forecasts similar growth (2.8%) as financial-conditions tailwinds fade but AI capex (front-loaded) and falling oil prices (toward $80) offset that. Downside risks: renewed Middle East escalation spiking oil, unsustainable fiscal paths (US, UK, especially France ahead of its April-May presidential election) tightening financial conditions, and AI capex deceleration (expected 2028-29 in baseline, timing uncertain) amid chip/memory shortages. Labor market: unemployment stable near 4.1-4.2%, but AI adoption is now visibly correlated with weaker employment growth across industries, with a temporary 0.5pp unemployment bump expected by 2028-29. Inflation overshot 2026 expectations mainly via tariff pass-through (~40bp to core PCE) and energy-driven airline fares; Goldman sees core PCE falling to 2.4% by end-2027 as both fade. The Fed hiked in September, will hike again in December (25bp expected), and Goldman expects one more hike in Q1 2027 -- fewer than markets price. ECB, BoE similarly seen hiking less than priced; BoJ seen hiking three times to a 2% terminal rate. Wilson argues bonds offer the best risk/reward since 2020, with yields grinding lower through 2027, and expects modest dollar softening, particularly versus the yen and yuan.
terms: PCE -- Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge
FOMC -- Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's rate-setting body
